===Etymology===
{{etymon|en|:inh|enm:moneye|tree=1}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*men- (think)}}
From {{inh|en|enm|moneye}}, {{m|enm|moneie}}, {{m|enm|money}}, borrowed from {{der|en|xno|muneie||money}}, from {{der|en|la|monēta||money, a place for coining money, coin, mint}}, from the name of the temple of Juno Moneta in Rome, where a mint was.

In this sense, displaced native {{ncog|ang|feoh}}, whence {{cog|en|fee}}. {{doublet|en|mint}}, ultimately from the same Latin word but through Germanic and Old English, and of {{m|en|manat}}, through Russian and Azerbaijani or Turkmen.

#: {{ux|en|Most animals are awake at day and sleep at '''night'''.}}
#* {{RQ:Rinehart Hopwood Bat|I|01|passage=The Bat—they called him the Bat. Like a bat he chose the '''night''' hours for his work of rapine; like a bat he struck and vanished, pouncingly, noiselessly; like a bat he never showed himself to the face of the day.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=2013-07-19|author=[http://www.theguardian.com/profile/iansample Ian Sample]
|volume=189|issue=6|page=34|magazine=w:The Guardian Weekly
|title=[http://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2013/jul/08/irregular-bedtimes-affect-childrens-brains Irregular bedtimes may affect children's brains]
|passage=Irregular bedtimes may disrupt healthy brain development in young children, according to a study of intelligence and sleeping habits.  ¶ Going to bed at a different time each '''night''' affected girls more than boys, but both fared worse on mental tasks than children who had a set bedtime, researchers found.}}
# {{lb|en|astronomy|countable}} The period of darkness beginning at the end of evening [[astronomical twilight]] when the sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, and ending at the beginning of morning astronomical twilight.
# {{lb|en|legal|countable}} A period of time often defined in the legal system as beginning 30 minutes after sunset, and ending 30 minutes before sunrise.
# {{lb|en|countable}} An [[evening]] or night spent at a particular activity.
#: {{ux|en|a '''night''' on the town}}
#: {{coi|en|game '''night'''}}
#: {{coi|en|[[girls' night out|girls' '''night''' out]]}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-06-08|volume=407|issue=8839|page=52
|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/international/21579039-chinas-growing-empire-ports-abroad-mainly-about-trade-not-aggression-new-masters The new masters and commanders]
|passage=From the ground, Colombo’s port does not look like much. Those entering it are greeted by wire fences, walls dating back to colonial times and security posts. For mariners leaving the port after lonely '''nights''' on the high seas, the delights of the B52 Night Club and Stallion Pub lie a stumble away.}}
# {{lb|en|countable}} A day, or at least a night.
#: {{ux|en|I stayed my friend's house for three '''nights'''.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} [[nightfall|Nightfall]].
#: {{ux|en|from noon till '''night'''}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} [[darkness|Darkness]] (due to it being [[nighttime]]).
#: {{ux|en|The cat disappeared into the '''night'''.}}
# {{lb|en|uncountable}} A dark [[blue]] colour, [[midnight blue]].
#: {{color panel|002266}}
# {{lb|en|sports|colloquial}} A night's worth of competitions, generally one game.

===Etymology 1===
{{wikidata lexeme|L42}}
{{etymon|en|id=response|:inh|enm:answere<id:noun>|tree=1}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂en-}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*h₂ent-|*swer-|id2=swear}}
From {{inh|en|enm|answere}}, {{m|enm|andsware}}, from {{inh|en|ang|andswaru||answer}}, from {{af|ang|and-|t1=against|swaru|t2=affirmation|nocat=1}}, (from {{der|en|ine-pro|*h₂ent-||front, forehead}} and {{der|en|ang|swerian||to swear}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*swer-}}), suggesting an original meaning of "a sworn statement rebutting a charge". The cognates suggest the existence of {{der|en|gem-pro|*andaswarō||a reply to a question}}. Cognate with {{cog|ofs|ondser||answer}}, {{cog|osx|andswōr||answer}}, {{cog|da|-}} and {{cog|sv|ansvar||liability, responsibility, answer}}, {{cog|is|andsvar||answer, response}}. Compare also {{cog|ang|andwyrde||answer}} (cognate to {{cog|nl|antwoord}}, {{cog|de|Antwort}}), {{cog|ang|andcwiss||reply}}, {{cog|de|Schwur||oath, vow}}.

From {{m|en|holla}}, {{m|en|hollo}} (attested 1588). This variant of {{m|en|hallo}} is often credited to {{w|Thomas Edison}} as a coinage for telephone use, but its appearance in print predates the invention of the telephone by several decades. Ultimately from a variant of {{der|en|ang|ēalā}}, such as {{m|ang|hēlā}}, which was used colloquially at the time similarly to how ''hey'' and (in some dialects) ''hi'' are used nowadays. Thus, equivalent to a compound of {{m|en|hey}} and {{m|en|lo}}. Used when drawing attention to yourself. Possibly influenced by {{ncog|osx|halo}}, {{lg|imperative}} of {{m|osx|halōn|t=to call, fetch}}, used in hailing a ferryman, akin to {{cog|goh|hala}}, {{m|goh|hola|hola!}}, imperative forms of {{m|goh|halōn}}, {{m|goh|holōn|t=to fetch}}. For more information, see {{l|en|hallo}}. The ''{{w|Oxford English Dictionary}}'' and ''{{w|Merriam-Webster Dictionary}}'' also suggested that it is a variant of {{m|en|holla}}, a variant of {{m|en|holloo}}. Further beyond, the origin remains uncertain. OED and Merriam-Webster suggested that it has a connection between {{m|en|hallow|t=to shout, to cry out loud}}, which came from Old French {{m|fro|holloer}}, which, according to ''Altfranzösisches Wörterbuch'', is from {{cog|osx|halōn}}. ===Pronunciation=== * {{enPR|hĕ-lō'|hə-lō'}} ** {{IPA|en|/hɛˈloʊ/|/hə-/|/ˈhɛloʊ/|a=GA}} ** {{a|en|UK}} *** {{IPA|en|/həˈləʊ/|/hɛ-/|a=RP}} **** {{audio|en|En-uk-hello.ogg|a=UK}} *** {{IPA|en|/haˈlaʊ/|a=Northumbrian}} ** {{IPA|en|/həˈləʉ/|a=AU}} *** {{audio|en|En-au-hello.ogg|a=AU}} ** {{IPA|en|/hɛˈloː/|/hə-/|/ˈhɛlo(ː)/|a=CA}} ** {{IPA|en|/həˈlo(w)/|a=Indic}} * {{rhymes|en|ɛləʊ|əʊ|s=2}} * {{hmp|en|hallow}} {| class="wikitable" ! =====Usage notes=====
* As with the names of {{l|en|lake|lakes}} and {{l|en|mountain|mountains}}, the names of rivers are typically formed by adding the word before or after the unique term: the {{m|en|River Thames}} or the {{m|en|Yangtze River}}. Generally speaking, names formed using adjectives or attributives see ''river'' added to the end, as with the {{m|en|Yellow River}}. It is less common to add ''river'' before names than it is with lakes, but many of the rivers of Britain are written that way, as with the {{m|en|River Severn}}; indeed, British English tends to use "River X" in such cases while American, South African, Australian and New Zealand English use "X River". The former derives from the earlier but now uncommon form ''river of ~'': the 19th century ''River of Jordan'' is now usually simply the ''River Jordan''.
* It is common to preface the proper names of rivers with the article {{m|en|the}}.
* Concerning the reference of its coordinate terms, some people say:<ref>[http://worldrivers.net/2018/11/29/distinction-of-rivers-stream-brooks-creeks-and-other-terms/ Definitions of rivers, stream, brooks, creeks and other terms] (Goran Šafarek, ''WorldRivers.net,'' November 29, 2018)</ref> you can step over a {{m|en|brook}}, jump over a {{m|en|creek}}, wade across a {{m|en|stream}}, and swim across a {{m|en||river}}.

====Usage notes====
* Usage of ''program'' and ''programme'':
** US: ''program'' is the only spelling normally used, no matter which sense it is used in.
** UK: ''programme'' is used in all cases except for computer code, in which case ''program'' has generally superseded ''programme'' since the 1960s. However, ''programme'' is still occasionally used for computer code, and some even consider it the only correct spelling also for this meaning.
** Canada: both ''program'' and ''programme'' are used, but ''program'' is more common.
** Australia: ''program'' is endorsed by the Macquarie Dictionary and is frequently used in both formal and informal settings.
** New Zealand: ''programme'' is favoured by New Zealand dictionaries, and is endorsed by government usage; ''program'' is rarely seen outside the computing meaning.
** Singapore and Malaysia: ''program'' and ''programme'' are interchangeable (the latter is more common), but only ''program'' is used in computing.

From {{inh|en|enm|questioun}}, from {{der|en|xno|questiun}}, from {{der|en|fro|question}}, from {{der|en|la|quaestiōnem}}, accusative of {{m|la|quaestiō||a seeking, investigation, inquiry, question}}, from {{m|la|quaerere||to seek, ask, inquire}},<ref name="Cent1911">{{R:Century}}</ref> of uncertain origin, but possibly from {{der|en|itc-pro|*kʷaizeō}}, from {{der|en|ine-pro|*kʷeh₂-||to acquire}}. {{doublet|en|quest}}.

|passage=Energy has seldom been found where we need it when we want it. Ancient nomads, wishing to ward off the '''evening''' chill and enjoy a meal around a campfire, had to collect wood and then spend time and effort coaxing the heat of friction out from between sticks to kindle a flame. With more settled people, animals were harnessed to capstans or caged in treadmills to turn grist into meal.}}
# The time of the day between the approximate time of midwinter dusk and midnight (compare [[afternoon]]); the period after the end of regular office working hours.
#* {{RQ:Besant Ivory Gate|III
|passage=At half-past nine on this Saturday '''evening''', the parlour of the Salutation Inn, High Holborn, contained most of its customary visitors.{{...}} In former days every tavern of repute kept such a room for its own select circle, a club, or society, of habitués, who met every '''evening''', for a pipe and a cheerful glass.}}
